reconcile.connective: Clarke reads the lion's dread as territorial avoidance — fleeing human settlements — rather than submission or retreat in a direct encounter.

discrepancy.connective: Christopher A. Baba's EvilBible.com — source of this exact question — sets Genesis's universal 'every beast' dread against Proverbs's fearless lion, which 'turneth not away for any.'

skeptic.name: Christopher A. Baba
skeptic.work: EvilBible.com, "Biblical Contradictions" (list entry: Genesis 9:2 vs. Proverbs 30:30, "Is every animal afraid of man?")
skeptic.attribution: Christopher A. Baba, editor, EvilBible.com (est. 2003), "Biblical Contradictions" list

excerpts.excerpt_text: Tigers, wolves, lions, and hyenas, the determinate foes of man, incapable of being tamed or domesticated, flee, through the principle of terror, from the dwelling of man, and thus he is providentially safe.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly names the lion among the beasts whose Gen 9:2 fear-response is cashed out as avoidance ('flee...from the dwelling of man') rather than tameable submission — supplies the 'avoidance, not submission-in-encounter' distinction defenders use to square the lion's boldness in Proverbs 30:30 with Genesis's universal dread-grant.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley catalogues this exact pairing by name — "Man's fear and dread upon all beasts. Not upon the lion. Gen. ix. 2. Prov. xxx. 30" — and then resolves it: "The second passage, 'A lion which is strongest among beasts, and turneth not away for any,' may mean, 'for any beast' — another way of designating the lion as the 'king of beasts.' If, however, it implies, 'for any man,' the exceptional cases which this statement covers only prove the general rule that the presence of man intimidates all the lower animals."

link.title: Is there a Bible contradiction in Proverbs 30:30?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of this exact verse pairing, citing Geisler & Howe's When Critics Ask (1992) for the same 'turns not away from other beasts' and 'exception proves the rule' arguments Haley gave in 1874.
